newsitem.title: USA: US prices still may be slipping-Clev Fed economist.
newsitem.headline: US prices still may be slipping-Clev Fed economist.

text.p: Measures of core U.S. inflation show the underlying price trend is not rising and may still be edging lower in a healthy U.S. economy, a Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland economist specializing in inflation said Tuesday.
"Can I see any upward trend in inflation? The answer is clearly no," economist Mychael Bryan told Reuters.
Bryan calculates the Cleveland Fed's monthly median Consumer Price Index, an alternative measure of core inflation, based on Bureau of Labor Statistics data.
Unlike core CPI, which excludes food and energy, median CPI eliminates any item whose behavior clearly departs from the performance of most CPI items in any given month.
The Cleveland Fed reported on Tuesday that median CPI rose 2.6 percent year-over-year in March, while core CPI was up 2.5 percent year-over-year.
The year-over-year trend in core CPI has held steady at around 2.5 percent over the past six months, while median CPI has drifted down to 2.6 percent from 2.8 in October.
Bryan works on median inflation measures with Ohio State University economist Stephen Cecchetti.
Cecchetti this summer will become director of research at the New York Fed, which is advocating targeting core measures of inflation to boost the credibility of monetary policy.
Cecchetti also will be the main policy adviser to New York Fed President William McDonough, the vice chairman of the Federal Open Market Committee.
"Median inflation measures are much less noisy and give a better idea of what the inflation trend is," said Bryan, who is collaborating with Cecchetti on refining measures of underlying inflation.

"I'm encouraged over the trend in median CPI that has been coming down a bit," Bryan said. "If this continues through the spring, I'll be ready to conclude the underlying inflation trend is moving still lower. We don't have enough evidence yet, but it's pointing in the right direction."

Bryan said there is no indication that CPI inflation is rising. If inflation data continue to come in as they have in recent months, the case could be made that inflation, "which has been pretty constant in the United States over the past five years, is still slipping," he said.
"There is no evidence the underlying trend of inflation is accelerating, and there is some evidence there is some moderation," said Bryan.
He said his work, like research conducted by other economists within the Fed System, is "not attempting to be a predictor of future monetary policy."
The Cleveland Fed economist acknowledged that a central bank should always be vigilant about inflation, while adding he does not subscribe to the notion that growth must result in higher prices.
"I'm of the school that thinks the way you promote growth is to produce a low rate of inflation," Bryan said.

"Those who have been promoting a low or stable price level should be encouraged by what we have seen on the investment side. That's the type of response people were hoping for," he added. He was referring to the declining inflation environment that allowed U.S. businesses to invest heavily in their sectors and allowed households to step up big-ticket item purchases.
Bryan said the relationship between tight labor markets and inflation was particularly tenuous.
"At any point in time, you can pick any particular industry with labor shortages. I am not sure this is predictive of higher inflation," he said.
Bryan said median CPI gives "a better idea of the inflation trend" but does not address the issue of how exact an inflation measure the CPI is.
